strengths: The paper establishes a clean and elegant theoretical connection between mutual information estimation and diffusion bridge matching/reciprocal processes, deriving an MI estimator as the difference of drifts of joint vs. independent reciprocal processes via the Girsanov theorem (Theorem 4.1), with a rigorous proof.

The theoretical framework is shown to generalize naturally to several related quantities: general KL divergence estimation, differential entropy estimation via information projections, pointwise mutual information, and interaction information (Appendices A.1-A.4), which broadens the potential utility of the approach.

The practical algorithm (InfoBridge) is described clearly with explicit training and inference procedures (Algorithms 1 and 2), including a useful practical trick of unifying the two drift networks with a binary conditioning input, which is shown empirically to improve accuracy.

Extensive empirical evaluation across a large low-dimensional benchmark suite (Czyz et al.) and challenging high-dimensional image-based benchmarks (Gaussians/Rectangles at 16x16 and 32x32), with comparisons against a good range of parametric and non-parametric baselines.

Honest and thorough discussion of limitations, including a dedicated additional experiment (Appendix B.3) showing that a leading baseline (AE+WKL) degrades sharply when its inductive-bias assumption (bottleneck dimensionality) is violated, strengthening the credibility of the comparison.
Good transparency in reporting experimental details, computational cost, architectures, and hyperparameters in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical machinery (reciprocal processes, Doob h-transform/conditional bridge matching, Girsanov-based KL decomposition) is largely adapted from existing diffusion bridge matching literature (e.g., Shi et al. 2023, De Bortoli et al. 2023) and closely parallels the MINDE approach (Franzese et al. 2024); the novelty is primarily in applying this known toolkit to MI estimation rather than introducing fundamentally new theory.

The claimed 'unbiasedness' of the estimator is a property of the population-level theorem assuming perfectly learned drifts; in practice the drifts are approximated by neural networks trained with finite data and SGD, so the practical algorithm inherits approximation bias/variance similar to other neural estimators (including MINDE, whose bias is instead controlled by a different, explicit term). This distinction is not sufficiently discussed or empirically quantified.

On the low-dimensional benchmark (Table 1/4), InfoBridge performs largely on par with MINDE and other baselines, with no case where it is clearly and substantially superior, undermining the significance of the low-dimensional results as a strong contribution.

In the image-data benchmark (Figure 1), which is presented as the paper's strongest result, MINDE—the most directly comparable and recent diffusion-based baseline discussed at length in Related Work—is conspicuously absent from the comparison, leaving an important gap in the empirical validation.

The Cauchy/heavy-tailed distribution failure case reveals a real limitation of the underlying bridge-matching framework, and while acknowledged, no mitigation beyond an ad hoc asinh transform is offered or evaluated rigorously (e.g., comparing tail-transform effects across methods).
Computational cost is stated to be 'comparable to MINDE,' but no direct runtime/sample-efficiency comparison table is given, making it hard to assess practical efficiency trade-offs.
Confidence intervals/variance are reported for the image benchmark but only point estimates are shown for the low-dimensional benchmark tables, limiting statistical rigor in that comparison.
The writing contains minor typos/grammatical issues (e.g., 'Theis type', inconsistent notation) that slightly detract from clarity.

strengths: The paper provides a clean theoretical derivation connecting mutual information to KL divergence between reciprocal processes, and via the disintegration and Girsanov theorems reduces MI estimation to a difference of Bridge-Matching drifts (Theorem 4.1); this derivation appears mathematically sound.

The framework is shown to generalize naturally to general KL divergence estimation, differential entropy estimation, pointwise MI, and interaction information, giving the paper a broader scope than a single-purpose estimator.

Experiments span both classical low-dimensional synthetic benchmarks (Czyz et al.) and more realistic image-manifold benchmarks (Butakov et al.), with a reasonably large set of baselines (MINDE, MINE, InfoNCE, NWJ, D-V, KSG, DoE, LNN, CCA, AE+WKL, N-MIENF).

The authors include a useful sanity-check ablation (Appendix B.3) showing that the AE+WKL baseline is highly sensitive to the choice of bottleneck dimensionality, which honestly contextualizes the comparison rather than merely declaring victory.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a re-application of already well-established machinery (reciprocal processes / Doob h-transform bridge matching, and the standard Girsanov-based KL decomposition between diffusions that MINDE and Schrodinger Bridge Matching papers already use) to the MI setting; the novelty over MINDE is thin, essentially swapping the object being matched (bridge drifts instead of denoising scores) while reusing the same KL-via-Girsanov argument.

Despite the claimed 'unbiasedness,' the practical estimator relies on finite-capacity neural network approximations of drifts trained with finite data, so the theoretical unbiasedness is not actually realized in the reported numbers; no bias/variance analysis of the neural approximation error is given, and the comparisons to MINDE's residual bias term are not made rigorous or quantitative.

On the low-dimensional benchmark (Tables 1 and 4), InfoBridge is essentially performance-neutral relative to MINDE across most distributions, with several entries where InfoBridge is actually worse (e.g., several multinormal/high-dimensional cases, Mn 50x50 dense, and various Spearman/Sp-transformed cases); the paper does not adequately explain or analyze these regressions, undermining the claimed 'comparable or superior' framing.

The heavy-tailed (Cauchy) failure case is acknowledged but not resolved, and it directly interacts with the paper's central 'unbiased' claim: the method is provably inapplicable in theory to a common class of distributions considered in the same benchmark suite, which is a significant limitation for a paper whose main selling point is unbiasedness.

The image benchmark uses only 3 seeds for InfoBridge (vs 5 for competing methods), and the strong claim that InfoBridge is 'the best among all bias-free estimators featured' is not well substantiated statistically given the small number of seeds and overlapping confidence intervals in Figure 1.

The architectural choice of a single shared network with a binary conditioning bit (Section 4.3) is justified only by an informal intuitive argument about matching approximation errors, without any controlled ablation comparing it against separate networks, leaving an important design decision underexplored.

Computational cost is only briefly mentioned as 'comparable to MINDE' without a systematic runtime/compute comparison table across all baselines, making it hard to assess practical trade-offs, especially given diffusion/bridge models are known to be expensive to train.

Overall the paper reads as an incremental, mostly theoretical repackaging of existing diffusion-bridge and Schrodinger-bridge machinery for MI estimation, with experimental results that mostly match (rather than clearly surpass) the closest prior work (MINDE), limiting its significance for a top-tier venue.

strengths: Clean and non-trivial theoretical contribution: the paper establishes a precise connection between mutual information and the KL divergence between reciprocal processes (mixtures of Brownian bridges), yielding an MI estimator expressed as a time-integral of squared drift differences (Theorem 4.1), with a clear proof via disintegration + Girsanov theorem.
The estimator is presented as free of the time-truncation/discretization bias present in the closest prior diffusion-based method (MINDE), which is a meaningful theoretical advantage.

Good generality: the framework is extended with relatively little extra effort to general KL divergence estimation, differential entropy estimation via exponential-family projections, pointwise MI, and interaction information (Appendix A), showing the approach is not a one-off trick.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation across two different benchmark families (low-dimensional tabular distributions from Czyż et al. and image-based manifold benchmarks from Butakov et al.), with results comparable to or better than strong existing baselines, including on high-dimensional image data.

Honest and useful discussion of limitations, e.g., the Cauchy/heavy-tailed distribution failure case is explained via the lack of a first moment, and the paper additionally shows (Appendix B.3) that a key competing baseline (AE+WKL 5-NN) is highly sensitive to a hyperparameter (bottleneck dimension) that is normally unknown in practice, strengthening the fairness of the comparison narrative.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed appendix with architectures, hyperparameters, training budgets, and compute cost for all baselines and the proposed method.
weaknesses: The 'unbiasedness' claim is only exact when the drift networks recover the true conditional expectations; in practice vjoint,ψ and vind,ϕ are imperfect MSE-trained approximations, and squaring imperfect estimates of a conditional expectation is a known source of bias (as MINDE and related methods also suffer from bias/variance trade-offs). The paper does not empirically or theoretically analyze the practical bias/variance behavior of the plug-in estimator, so the 'unbiased' framing may be overstated relative to what is demonstrated.

MINDE, the most directly comparable diffusion-based baseline and the one explicitly contrasted with in the theory/related work section, is omitted from the image-benchmark comparison (Figure 1), which is the setting where the paper's headline claims of superiority are made; this is a significant gap in the empirical narrative.

The image experiments are limited to synthetic, low-intrinsic-dimensionality manifolds (Gaussians/Rectangles) rather than real image data, so the claimed relevance to realistic high-dimensional settings (e.g., text-to-image alignment, SSL) is not directly validated.

No error bars/confidence intervals are reported in the main low-dimensional benchmark tables (only mean estimates), making it hard to assess estimator variance and statistical significance of differences versus MINDE and other baselines.

The practical algorithm requires training generative bridge-matching models (comparable cost to MINDE), which is expensive relative to lighter discriminative estimators (MINE/InfoNCE); computational cost/scalability trade-offs are only briefly mentioned rather than systematically studied.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental in that it largely repurposes existing bridge-matching/Schrödinger-bridge machinery (already used by MINDE and others for KL/generative modeling) for the specific MI use case, rather than introducing fundamentally new bridge-matching methodology.

strengths: Novel and rigorous theoretical connection between reciprocal processes/diffusion bridge matching and mutual information estimation, yielding an estimator (Theorem 4.1) that is unbiased in principle (unlike MINDE, which has a bias term that only vanishes as T→∞).
Clean proofs leveraging disintegration and Girsanov theorems, and useful extensions (KL divergence, differential entropy, interaction information) that broaden the applicability of the framework.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three regimes: low-dimensional synthetic benchmarks, image-based manifold benchmarks, and real-world protein language model embeddings.

Strong and consistent performance advantage over MINDE and other generative/discriminative baselines on the image and protein benchmarks, including cases where MINDE catastrophically overestimates MI.

Careful and honest comparison methodology, e.g., pointing out that competing methods (AE+WKL, MIENF) rely on inductive biases (known intrinsic dimensionality or Gaussianizable structure) that InfoBridge does not require, and demonstrating (Appendix C.5) that AE+WKL's performance degrades sharply without this prior knowledge.
Useful ablation studies on volatility coefficient ε and network size showing reasonable robustness of the method.
Transparent limitations section acknowledging failure on heavy-tailed (Cauchy) distributions and high sample/compute requirements.
weaknesses: On the low-dimensional benchmark, InfoBridge is only comparable to existing methods (MINDE) rather than clearly superior, tempering the overall claim of superiority.

The core methodological idea is closely related to MINDE (drift/score matching + Girsanov-based KL decomposition); the main novelty is substituting the diffusion bridge (reciprocal process) formulation for standard forward/backward diffusion, which is a comparatively incremental technical extension despite yielding practical benefits.

The theoretical framework relies on finite first-moment assumptions, which is a real limitation for heavy-tailed data that are common in practice (e.g., Cauchy-like distributions), and mitigations (asinh transform) are only partially explored.

The 'unifying binary input' trick for parametrizing the two drifts with a single network is justified only empirically/heuristically, without deeper analysis of why or when it helps versus separate networks.
Image benchmark results are averaged over only 3 seeds (vs. 5 for baselines), which weakens the statistical robustness of the comparison somewhat.

The 'real-world' evaluation is limited to a single dataset (protein embeddings) with an MI ground truth constructed via a synthetic class-label-sharing procedure, so it does not fully demonstrate applicability to genuinely unconstrained real-world data.

Computational cost (training two conditional bridge matching models, sampling procedures) is not thoroughly compared against baselines in the main text, only briefly mentioned in the appendix, leaving practical scalability underexplored.

strengths: The paper establishes a clean theoretical link between mutual information estimation and diffusion bridge matching/reciprocal processes, deriving an MI decomposition (Theorem 4.1) that, unlike MINDE, does not require an infinite-time truncation and hence removes MINDE's bias term.

Evaluation spans three distinct benchmark types (low-dimensional synthetic distributions, image-based manifold benchmarks, and real protein language model embeddings), which is a reasonably broad testbed compared to many MI-estimator papers.
On the protein embedding benchmark, InfoBridge is clearly the best performer while MINDE-C/J catastrophically diverge (MAE 9.29/1342 vs 0.04), providing a genuinely convincing real-world result.

The paper includes useful generalizations (KL divergence, differential entropy, interaction information) and ablations on volatility coefficient and network size, showing some robustness of the method to hyperparameters.
The related work section is thorough and clearly categorizes existing MI estimators, helping to contextualize the contribution.
weaknesses: On the low-dimensional benchmark (Table 1/9), InfoBridge's performance is essentially indistinguishable from MINDE across most test cases, undercutting the claim that the removal of the theoretical bias term yields a practically superior estimator; the benefit seems mostly theoretical rather than empirically demonstrated.

On the image benchmark, the paper's own framing concedes that competing methods (MIENF, AE+WKL) achieve comparable or better accuracy but rely on inductive bias/prior knowledge (e.g., matching intrinsic dimensionality); InfoBridge is only claimed to be 'best among inductive-bias-free estimators,' a narrower and weaker claim than 'superior performance' stated in the contributions.

The core theoretical machinery (disintegration theorem, Girsanov-based KL between diffusions, conditional bridge matching) is largely assembled from existing results in diffusion bridge/Schrödinger bridge literature (Léonard, Shi et al., Zhou et al.); the main novel step is substituting the reciprocal-process/bridge formulation for MINDE's forward/backward diffusion formulation, which is an incremental rather than fundamentally new methodological advance.

The method inherits known limitations of bridge matching: failure on heavy-tailed (no first moment) distributions such as the Cauchy case, and reliance on relatively large training sets, which the authors acknowledge but do not substantially address beyond an ad hoc asinh transform.

The practical 'shared network with binary conditioning input' trick, which the authors report is important for accurate MI estimates, is justified only heuristically/empirically rather than theoretically, leaving open questions about why and when it helps or could fail.

Statistical support for the image benchmark claims is somewhat weak: only 3-5 seeds are used, and Figure 1 shows overlapping confidence intervals among several methods, making the claimed ranking less conclusive.

Appendix results such as the entropy estimation experiments (Fig. 3) and the interaction information extension are only illustrative (single runs, no baselines), so it's unclear how reliable or competitive these generalizations actually are.

The computational cost of training diffusion bridge models (tens of GPU-hours per seed reported in the appendix) is high relative to classical/discriminative baselines, and the paper does not provide a clear cost-benefit discussion of when this overhead is justified given the largely comparable performance in several benchmarks.

strengths: Novel and elegant theoretical connection between reciprocal processes / diffusion bridge matching and mutual information estimation, expressed as a clean drift-difference formula (Theorem 4.1) with a rigorous proof via disintegration and Girsanov-type KL decomposition.

The theory naturally generalizes beyond MI to general KL divergence estimation, differential entropy estimation, and interaction information, giving the framework broader applicability than a single-purpose estimator.

Thorough empirical evaluation across three qualitatively different regimes: low-dimensional analytic benchmarks, high-dimensional image-manifold benchmarks, and real-world protein language model embeddings, which is a more comprehensive test suite than most competing MI estimator papers.

Strong empirical results on the harder benchmarks: the method is competitive with or better than MINDE on low-dimensional data and clearly superior to MINDE and other neural/classical baselines on image and protein embedding benchmarks, while avoiding inductive biases used by top competing methods (MIENF's Gaussianizability assumption, AE+WKL's oracle bottleneck dimension).

Careful and honest limitations discussion (heavy-tailed/no-first-moment distributions such as Cauchy, high data requirements) and transparent ablations on volatility coefficient ε and network size showing reasonable robustness.
Good engineering discussion (unified network with binary conditioning input to reduce variance of drift differences) that is a nice practical trick supported by an empirical ablation.
weaknesses: The estimator is only theoretically unbiased under exact drift recovery; with realistic finite-capacity neural network approximation, the estimator inherits approximation bias analogous to score-based methods like MINDE, and this gap between the theoretical unbiasedness claim and practical behavior is not deeply analyzed (e.g., no bias-vs-approximation-error study analogous to MINDE's discretization bias analysis).

Optimal ε varies noticeably across datasets in the ablation (image benchmark best around 0.01–0.03, protein data best around 1), yet the paper fixes ε=1 uniformly for consistency, potentially leaving performance on the table and raising concerns about hyperparameter sensitivity/tuning cost in new domains.

On the low-dimensional benchmark (arguably the most rigorously validated regime with tractable ground truth), InfoBridge performance is essentially on par with MINDE rather than clearly superior, so the strongest quantitative gains are concentrated in the image and protein settings, which are harder to independently verify.

Fewer random seeds are used for InfoBridge (3) than for most baselines (5) in the image benchmark, and computational cost (GPU-hours) is substantial (6–18 GPU-hours per single run) but not directly compared against baseline costs in a unified cost-accuracy tradeoff discussion.

The protein embedding MI construction (shared-label-only dependency) is a fairly synthetic proxy for "real-world" dependency and may not fully capture the complexity of naturally occurring high-dimensional dependencies; MINDE's dramatic failure on this benchmark (MAE ~9-1342) is surprising and warrants more diagnosis to rule out implementation/calibration issues rather than an inherent limitation of diffusion-score-based KL estimation.

The paper does not compare against other recent scalable MI estimation approaches such as sliced mutual information variants, which are cited in related work but omitted from the empirical comparison tables, leaving open how InfoBridge compares to a wider set of modern high-dimensional MI estimators.
